method_card.title: Half-Life and Nuclear Equations
steps: Half-life: find n = total time ÷ half-life, then halve the activity n times (never divide by n).
Going back in time, double the activity once for each half-life instead of halving.
Alpha decay: mass number − 4, atomic number − 2. The alpha particle is \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\).
Beta decay: mass number unchanged, atomic number + 1. The beta particle is an electron.
method_card.content:
Half-life is the time for the activity of a source to halve. To find the activity after a time t, work out n = t ÷ half-life, then halve the starting activity n times. Never divide the activity by n itself.

To go backwards in time, double the activity once for each half-life instead of halving.

Nuclear equations must balance: the mass numbers on each side must add up, and so must the atomic numbers. Alpha decay drops the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2. Beta decay leaves the mass number the same and raises the atomic number by 1. Check whether your board gives you the particle symbols.

exam_context.frequency: High: half-life calculations and nuclear equation balancing appear every year in higher-tier physics

gold.display: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5 years. A sample currently has an activity of 50 Bq. Calculate the activity 25 years ago.

misconceptions.message: Going back 25 years is 5 half-lives earlier, when activity was higher: 50 × 2⁵ = 1600 Bq. Halving instead (50 ÷ 32) gives about 1.56 Bq, which is the future, not the past.

gold.hint: Going back in time, double the activity once for each half-life.

guided_steps.say: Going back in time, the activity was higher. Each half-life earlier it was double. First find how many half-lives fit in 25 years.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the time by the half-life.

guided_steps.done: Five doublings back through time.
Halving 5 times (÷32) returns 50 Bq now, so 1600 Bq is right.

guided_steps.say: So the activity 25 years ago was 1600 Bq.

gold.display: Thorium-234 undergoes beta decay. Its mass number is 234 and atomic number is 90. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?

misconceptions.message: Beta decay raises the atomic number by 1: 90 + 1 = 91 (protactinium). Lowering it to 89 goes the wrong way.

gold.hint: Beta decay leaves the mass number alone and adds 1 to the atomic number.

guided_steps.say: Beta decay: the mass number stays the same and the atomic number rises by 1 (a neutron becomes a proton).

guided_steps.done: Daughter is protactinium-234: atomic number 91, mass number 234.
guided_steps.hint: Beta decay leaves the mass number unchanged.

guided_steps.say: So the daughter's atomic number is 91.

gold.display: Polonium-210 undergoes alpha decay. Its atomic number is 84. What is the mass number of the daughter nucleus? (Mass number of Po-210 = 210)

misconceptions.message: Alpha decay lowers the mass number by 4: 210 − 4 = 206. Subtracting 2 (the atomic-number change) gives 208, mixing the two up.

gold.hint: Alpha decay lowers the mass number by 4.

guided_steps.say: Alpha decay: the mass number drops by 4 and the atomic number drops by 2.

guided_steps.pre: Nucleons carried off by the alpha particle =

guided_steps.done: Daughter is lead-206: mass number 206, atomic number 82.

guided_steps.say: So the daughter's mass number is 206.

gold.display: A sample of iodine-131 (half-life = 8 days) has an initial activity of 5120 Bq. How many days does it take for the activity to fall to 160 Bq?

misconceptions.message: Five halvings take you from 5120 to 160 Bq, so n = 5. But the question asks for time: 5 × 8 = 40 days. Answering 5 gives the number of half-lives, not the time.

gold.hint: Count how many halvings reach 160 Bq, then multiply by the half-life.

guided_steps.say: Halve from 5120 Bq until you reach 160 Bq, counting the steps. Each step is one half-life.

guided_steps.done: Reached 160 Bq.

guided_steps.pre: Count the halving steps you did: n =
guided_steps.hint: How many times did you divide by 2?

guided_steps.done: 40 days.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply the number of half-lives by the half-life.

guided_steps.done: 5 halvings (÷32) reach 160 Bq, so 40 days is right.

guided_steps.say: So it takes 40 days.

gold.display: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 3200 Bq and a half-life of 10 minutes. What is the activity after 50 minutes?

misconceptions.message: n = 5, halve five times: 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq. Dividing 3200 by 5 gives 640, which is not halving.

gold.hint: Find n = 50 ÷ 10, then halve five times.

guided_steps.say: Find n first: n = total time ÷ half-life.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the time by the half-life.

guided_steps.done: Five halvings done.
That is 100 × 2⁵ = 3200 Bq, so 100 Bq is right.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 100 Bq.

bronze.display: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 400 Bq. Calculate the activity after 1 half-life.

misconceptions.message: One half-life halves the activity: 400 ÷ 2 = 200 Bq. Doubling to 800 goes the wrong way.

bronze.hint: One half-life means halve the activity once.

guided_steps.say: One half-life is the time for the activity to halve. Start at 400 Bq.

guided_steps.pre: How many times does the sample halve here? Number of half-lives =
guided_steps.hint: The question says after one half-life.

guided_steps.done: Back to 400 Bq, so 200 Bq after one half-life is right.
guided_steps.hint: Doubling should return the starting activity.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 200 Bq.

bronze.display: A sample has an initial activity of 1600 Bq. Calculate the activity after 2 half-lives.

misconceptions.message: Two half-lives means halving twice: 1600 → 800 → 400 Bq. Stopping after one halving leaves 800.

bronze.hint: Two half-lives: halve, then halve again.

guided_steps.say: Two half-lives means the activity halves twice. Start at 1600 Bq.

guided_steps.hint: The question says after two half-lives.

guided_steps.done: Two halvings done.
Back to 1600 Bq, so 400 Bq is right.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 400 Bq.

bronze.display: A sample has an initial activity of 800 Bq. Calculate the activity after 3 half-lives.

misconceptions.message: Three half-lives means halving three times: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq. Stopping at two halvings leaves 200.

bronze.hint: Halve three times, one step at a time.

guided_steps.say: Three half-lives means halving three times. Start at 800 Bq.

guided_steps.hint: The question says after three half-lives.

guided_steps.done: Three halvings done.
Back to 800 Bq, so 100 Bq is right.
guided_steps.hint: Doubling three times returns the start.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 100 Bq.

bronze.display: What fraction of the original activity remains after 4 half-lives?

misconceptions.message: Four half-lives multiplies the fraction by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 = 0.0625. Writing 1 ÷ (2 × 4) = 0.125 treats the halvings as one division.

bronze.hint: Multiply by one half for each half-life: (1/2) four times.

guided_steps.say: Each half-life leaves half as much. Start with the whole sample as a fraction: 1.

guided_steps.hint: The question says after four half-lives.

guided_steps.done: That is 1/16 of the original.

guided_steps.say: So 1/16 (0.0625) of the activity remains.

bronze.display: In alpha decay, by how much does the mass number decrease?

misconceptions.message: An alpha particle carries away 4 nucleons (2 protons + 2 neutrons), so the mass number drops by 4. The atomic number is what drops by 2.

bronze.hint: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\).

guided_steps.say: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, written \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\). Count what it takes away.

guided_steps.done: The mass number counts nucleons, so it drops by 4.

guided_steps.say: So the mass number decreases by 4.

bronze.display: In beta decay, by how much does the atomic number change?
bronze.equation_hint: A neutron converts to a proton + electron

misconceptions.message: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton, so the atomic number rises by 1. A change of 2 is alpha decay, not beta.

bronze.hint: In beta decay a neutron turns into a proton.

guided_steps.say: In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron. The electron leaves as the beta particle.

guided_steps.pre: Atomic number counts protons, so it changes by =
Mass number change (a neutron just became a proton, total nucleons the same) =
guided_steps.done: Atomic number goes up by 1; mass number is unchanged.

guided_steps.say: So the atomic number changes by 1 (it increases).

silver.display: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample has an initial activity of 640 Bq. Calculate the activity after 32 days.
silver.equation_hint: n = total time ÷ half-life, then halve n times

misconceptions.message: n = 4 half-lives means halving four times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 → 40 Bq. Dividing 640 by 4 gives 160, treating four halvings as one division.

silver.hint: Find n = time ÷ half-life first, then halve n times.

guided_steps.say: First find n, the number of half-lives: n = total time ÷ half-life.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the total time by the half-life.

guided_steps.done: Four halvings done.
That is 40 × 2⁴ = 640 Bq, the start, so 40 Bq is right.
guided_steps.hint: 2⁴ = 16; multiplying back should give the start.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 40 Bq.

silver.display: A radioactive sample starts with an activity of 2400 Bq. Its half-life is 6 hours. Calculate the activity after 18 hours.

misconceptions.message: n = 3, so halve three times: 2400 → 1200 → 600 → 300 Bq. Dividing 2400 by 3 gives 800, which is not how halving works.

silver.hint: Work out how many half-lives fit in 18 hours, then halve that many times.

guided_steps.say: Find n first: n = total time ÷ half-life.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the total time by the half-life.

guided_steps.done: Three halvings done.
That is 300 × 2³ = 2400 Bq, so 300 Bq is right.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 300 Bq.

silver.display: Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay. Its atomic number is 92. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
silver.equation_hint: Alpha decay: atomic number decreases by 2

misconceptions.message: Alpha decay lowers the atomic number by 2: 92 − 2 = 90 (thorium). Subtracting 4 (the mass-number change) gives 88, mixing the two up.

silver.hint: Alpha decay lowers the atomic number by 2.

guided_steps.say: Alpha decay emits \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\): the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

guided_steps.done: 2 protons lost, so the daughter has atomic number 90 (thorium).

guided_steps.say: So the daughter's atomic number is 90.

silver.display: Carbon-14 undergoes beta decay. Its mass number is 14 and atomic number is 6. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
silver.equation_hint: Beta decay: atomic number increases by 1

misconceptions.message: Beta decay raises the atomic number by 1: 6 + 1 = 7 (nitrogen). Lowering it to 5 goes the wrong way; a neutron becomes a proton, adding one.

silver.hint: Beta decay raises the atomic number by 1.

guided_steps.say: Beta decay: a neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleus gains one proton.

guided_steps.pre: Mass number stays the same at =
guided_steps.done: Atomic number 7 (nitrogen), mass number unchanged at 14.
guided_steps.hint: Beta decay does not change the mass number.

guided_steps.say: So the daughter's atomic number is 7.

silver.display: A sample of a radioactive isotope has a half-life of 4 years. If the initial activity is 960 Bq, what is the activity after 20 years?

misconceptions.message: n = 5, halve five times: 960 → 480 → 240 → 120 → 60 → 30 Bq. Dividing 960 by 5 gives 192, treating five halvings as one division.

silver.hint: Find n = 20 ÷ 4, then halve the activity n times.

guided_steps.say: Find n first: n = total time ÷ half-life.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the total time by the half-life.

guided_steps.done: Five halvings done.
That is 30 × 2⁵ = 960 Bq, so 30 Bq is right.

guided_steps.say: So the activity is 30 Bq.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One half-life at a time: halve the activity, or recall the alpha and beta decay rules.
problem_bank.silver_description: Find the number of half-lives first (n = time ÷ half-life), then halve that many times.
problem_bank.gold_description: Multi-step problems: work backwards in time, find an unknown time, or balance a decay.

bronze.title: Bronze: one halving at a time
steps: Activity halves every half-life. After each half-life, divide the activity by 2.
When the question tells you the number of half-lives, just halve that many times.
For decay: an alpha particle is \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\); a beta particle is an electron. Check whether your board gives you these symbols.

example.question: A sample of 320 Bq decays. Find the activity after 3 half-lives.

silver.title: Silver: find n first, then halve
steps: First find n, the number of half-lives: n = total time ÷ half-life.
Then halve the activity n times. Never divide the activity by n; that is the classic slip.
For decay: alpha lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2; beta raises the atomic number by 1 and leaves the mass number unchanged.

example.question: A source has a half-life of 5 days and an initial activity of 800 Bq. Find the activity after 15 days.

gold.title: Gold: multi-step and working backwards
steps: Chain two ideas: find n, then halve (or double) that many times.
Going backwards in time, activity was higher, so double for each half-life instead of halving.
To find a time, count how many halvings reach the target activity, then multiply n by the half-life.

example.question: Radon-222 undergoes alpha decay (atomic number 86, mass number 222). Give the daughter's mass number and atomic number.

opener.label: Before any physics
opener.display:
A glow stick loses half its brightness every hour.
It starts at 80 units of brightness.

steps.say: No physics yet, just common sense. Half the brightness is gone after one hour.
Another hour goes by, so it halves again.

That fixed time for the amount to halve is called the half-life. Radioactive activity works exactly the same way: each half-life, halve the activity. To find the amount after several half-lives, just halve again and again.

bronze.label: Halving a known number of times
bronze.display: A sample has an activity of 240 Bq. Find the activity after 2 half-lives.

steps.say: Each half-life halves the activity. Here we halve twice.

steps.hint: The question says after two half-lives.

steps.done: Back to 240 Bq, so 60 Bq is right.

silver.label: Find n from the time, then halve
silver.display: A source has a half-life of 3 hours and an initial activity of 4800 Bq. Find the activity after 12 hours.

steps.say: The time is given, not the number of half-lives. Find n first.

gold.label: Working backwards in time
gold.display: A sample now reads 12 Bq. Its half-life is 2 years. What was the activity 8 years ago?

steps.say: Going back in time, the activity was higher, so double for each half-life. Find n first.

steps.done: Four doublings back, so 192 Bq eight years ago.

steps.say: So the activity was 192 Bq eight years ago.
